Section: 2.2 Agent Communication Establishment

Here, we present studies on communication establishment that can be applied on different agents, regardless of the (in-)formal system each agent operates under.
Communication Establishment in Open Multi-Agent Systems. OMASfocuses on agent interaction in dynamic populations of agents. Computationally this means that neither the agents' system, nor the task that they will need to perform, can be decided a priori. Therefore, the agents need to learn how to communicate while making the least amount of assumptions regarding other agents. To that end, communication or symbol alignments is established according to environment observations, that is grounded communication.
In [3], the agents engage in a conversation, which both interpret according to their own automaton. Some of the communication language is shared, and the rest of the symbols are aligned after enough interactions. The communication is considered to be successful if the agents end the conversation at the same time, which is an observable act and inline with our approach, but ignores the actual outcome. Our framework requires the agents to perform an action, i.e. answer a query, to better estimate the levels of correct communication. Experiments of that study were performed on synthetically generated automata.
In [16], a set of agents learn how to interact with each other in order to achieve potentially conflicting goals. The communicated symbols are interpreted in terms of the agent's observable actions that follow. Agents decide what to communicate aiming to decrease interpretation entropy, but can also misuse a word as an attempt to take advantage of other agents. In this approach, agent communication is not explicitly interpreted, but indirectly affects the agent behavior, via training a Markov Decision Process that translates communication events into actions, based on environmental rewards. While this study does not focus on communication establishment, it follows our framework idea that agent learning should be based on indirect environmental rewards.
Language Games. Language games [18] are an approach to establish successful communication in an OMAS only via grounded communication. In this setup, a population of agents engage in pairs to play grounded referential games. In these games, the agents develop their own vocabulary, that is interpreted in terms of object characteristics and is used to refer to a particular object in a context. After enough games, the population of agents converges to having shared symbol interpretations, allowing them to always communicate successfully. This work has been extended to scenarios where one agent teaches the other one how to interpret natural language questions regarding a commonly perceived scene of objects [13]. Additionally, there has also been a demonstration on how a human can engage with a computer to teach it a concept, by constructing examples using physical world objects [14]. These studies have a different focus compared to our work. They aim to replicate the humane ability of developing a language through de-centralized peer-to-peer interactions. The main aim of these studies is to study the evolution of natural languages, by replicating the process. In more detail, the agents interact in multiple random scenarios of having to refer to an object in their surrounding using invented words. Eventually they converge to a commonly interpreted vocabulary that allows them to successfully communicate in any scenario. On the other hand, our framework is designed for learning to communicate one specific concept, as efficiently as possible, by designing interaction contexts, i.e. the teaching examples, accordingly.
Interactive Reinforcement Learning. There have also been some studies that do not aim to establish human-computer communication, but use a human in the loop to create more efficient Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods. RL studies categories of problems where the reward signal is sparse and is only provided to the agent after multiple decisions. Such algorithms are very computationally expensive as they usually require a lot of action-reward exploration. Interactive RL aims to incorporate human input in that process, in order to make the convergence of such approaches faster [5]. This way, interactive RL studies focus on the downstream task, and use human input as a way to improve their performance.

Establishing Shared Query Understanding in an Open Multi-Agent System

Abstract: We propose a method that allows to develop shared understanding between two agents for the purpose of performing a task that requires cooperation. Our method focuses on efficiently establishing successful task-oriented communication in an open multi-agent system, where the agents do not know anything about each other and can only communicate via grounded interaction. The method aims to assist researchers that work on human-machine interaction or scenarios that require a human-in-the-loop, by defining interaction restrictions and efficiency metrics. To that end, we point out the challenges and limitations of such a (diverse) setup, while also restrictions and requirements which aim to ensure that high task performance truthfully reflects the extent to which the agents correctly understand each other. Furthermore, we demonstrate a use-case where our method can be applied for the task of cooperative query answering. We design the experiments by modifying an established ontology alignment benchmark. In this example, the agents want to query each other, while representing different databases, defined in their own ontologies that contain different and incomplete knowledge. Grounded interaction here has the form of examples that consists of common instances, for which the agents are expected to have similar knowledge. Our experiments demonstrate successful communication establishment under the required restrictions, and compare different agent policies that aim to solve the task in an efficient manner.

input: How do decentralized AI agents enhance collaborative decision-making through agent-to-agent communication and verifiable identities?
actual_output:
Decentralized AI agents enhance collaborative decision-making by leveraging agent-to-agent communication and verifiable identities, which facilitate secure and trusted interactions across organizational boundaries. The integration of Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and Verifiable Credentials (VCs) allows these agents to establish mutual trust and authenticate each other autonomously.

In a multi-agent ecosystem, agents equipped with self-sovereign digital identities can engage in dialogues that extend beyond isolated environments. For instance, while one agent may assist a user in planning a vacation, it can collaborate with other agents from travel agencies, airlines, and hotels to execute the entire booking process. This collaborative capability is crucial for tasks that exceed the scope of individual agents, enabling them to work together effectively to achieve complex goals [1. arXiv:2511.02841v2].

The use of DIDs and VCs provides a framework for agents to prove their identities and capabilities without relying on centralized authorities. Each agent can present verifiable credentials that encode claims about its identity and authorizations, which are cryptographically signed and tamper-resistant. This decentralized approach mitigates risks associated with data centralization and unauthorized access, thereby enhancing privacy and security [2. arXiv:2511.02841v2]. 

Moreover, the experimental setup described in the paper demonstrates that agents can autonomously authenticate each other and establish diverse trust relationships through the exchange of VCs, which can be anchored in a distributed ledger. This mechanism not only supports intra-domain interactions but also enables cross-domain verifiability, allowing agents to issue and verify credentials across different contexts [5. arXiv:2511.02841v2].

In summary, decentralized AI agents enhance collaborative decision-making by enabling secure, trusted interactions through verifiable identities, allowing them to work together effectively in complex, multi-agent environments.

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Abstract: A fundamental limitation of current LLM-based AI agents is their inability to build differentiated trust among each other at the onset of an agent-to-agent dialogue. However, autonomous and interoperable trust establishment becomes essential once agents start to operate beyond isolated environments and engage in dialogues across individual or organizational boundaries. A promising way to fill this gap in Agentic AI is to equip agents with long-lived digital identities and introduce tamper-proof and flexible identity-bound attestations of agents, provisioned by commonly trusted third parties and designed for cross-domain verifiability. This article presents a conceptual framework and a prototypical multi-agent system, where each agent is endowed with a self-sovereign digital identity. It combines a unique and ledger-anchored W3C Decentralized Identifier (DID) of an agent with a set of third-party issued W3C Verifiable Credentials (VCs). This enables agents at the start of a dialog to prove ownership of their self-controlled DIDs for authentication purposes and to establish various cross-domain trust relationships through the spontaneous exchange of their self-hosted DID-bound VCs. A comprehensive evaluation of the prototypical implementation demonstrates technical feasibility but also reveals limitations once an agent's LLM is in sole charge to control the respective security procedures.

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Section: 3 Related Work

Equipping agents with DIDs and VCs has recently attracted significant attention as a foundation for secure and privacy-preserving identity management in multi- agent ecosystems. Chaffer et al. (Chaffer et al., 2024) present the ETHOS framework, which adopts the SSI paradigm for agents. Their work highlights benefits in terms of privacy preservation, risk classification, and compliance record management. By leveraging decentralized identity technologies, ETHOS mitigates risks associated with data centralization and unauthorized access, while simultaneously supporting regulatory audits and compliance. South et al. (South et al., 2025) discuss mechanisms for authenticated delegation among agents. They investigate the sole use of VCs or in combination with OIDC to identify agents and to share verifiable delegations. The LOKA protocol proposed by Ranjan et al. (Ranjan et al., 2025) introduces a framework for ethically governed agent ecosystems. Central to this design is a Universal Agent Identity Layer that leverages DIDs and VCs to establish interoperable and verifiable agent identities. Huang et al. (Huang et al., 2025) propose a zerotrust identity framework built on verifiable agent identities using DIDs and VCs, directly addressing shortcomings of conventional identity and access management systems such as static trust models and limited delegation. Their research highlights how these decentralized mechanisms can create robust, contextsensitive trust and authorization, better suited for dynamic, multi-agent environments. The Agent Network protocol (ANP) also leverages DIDs as a mechanism to uniquely identify agents (Chang et al., 2025). Unlike ledger-based approaches, ANP anchors DIDs in centrally managed web servers, reflecting a pragmatic but less decentralized design choice. The Networked Agents and Decentralized AI (NANDA) index's integration of DIDs and VCs for agents is underpinned by the AgentFacts model, which provides a structured, machine-readable template for representing agent identity and capabilities (Raskar et al., 2025). This approach allows registries and clients to validate agent authenticity, assess reputation, and facilitate dynamic trust evaluation. Other noteworthy contributions include Hossen et al.'s secure communication framework for decentralized agents (Hossen et al., 2025) and Zou et al.'s BlockA2A protocol for secure, verifiable agent-to-agent interoperability (Zou et al., 2025).
In contrast, our approach integrates the VC exchange directly into the A2A protocol. By employing the DIF presentation proof protocol 3 in combination with JSON-LD-encoded VCs on top of A2A, our design extends an existing agent-to-agent interoperability mechanism with built-in trust establishment based on standardized protocols and formats from the domain of decentralized identity management.
3 https://identity.foundation/presentation-exchange/

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Section: 1 INTRODUCTION

The advent of LLM-based AI agents has opened new opportunities for enhancing human productivity and decision-making (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025). A single agent can autonomously retrieve information, perform calculations, automate workflows, and interface with digital services on behalf of its user. Such capabilities already demonstrate tangible benefits in personal assistance and task execution. However, the true potential of agents emerges when they are able to interact and collaborate among each other across organizational boundaries (Sharma et al., 2025). Through agent-to-agent communication, tasks that exceed the scope of an individual agent can be accomplished collaboratively. For instance, while one agent may support a user in planning a vacation by identifying preferences and budget constraints, it is only through secure and trusted interaction with external agents of travel agencies, airlines, and hotels that the full process of planning and booking a holiday can be autonomously and firmly executed.

This shift from isolated single-agent operation to cross-domain multi-agent collaboration comes with new challenges such as interoperability (Sharma et al., 2025), security (Ko et al., 2025) (Kong et al., 2025) (Schroeder de Witt, 2025), and trust (Huang et al., 2025) (Raza et al., 2025). An important step toward addressing interoperability is the recently published Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol 1 , which provides a standardized interaction layer among agents that remains agnostic to the underlying agent frameworks. Enhanced with payment capabilities as introduced by Vaziry et al. (Vaziry et al., 2025) and later implemented by AP2 2 , it may mark the start of agents to become economic actors. In terms of security, A2A builds upon well-established and widely deployed mechanisms from the Web ecosystem, e.g., TLS with x.509 certificates or OpenIDConnect (OIDC).
1 https://a2a-protocol.org
2 https://github.com/google-agentic-commerce/AP2
However, the reliance on traditional web security also carries over its inherent limitations. Web-based access control was originally designed for humancentric use cases, where end-users explicitly initiate sessions, consent to access, and manage credentials. In contrast, agents are expected to operate autonomously and at scale, which exposes shortcomings such as limited support for delegation of authority, insufficient contextualization of trust decisions, and reliance on static trust models that fail to adapt dynamically to a changing context (Huang et al., 2025). These constraints highlight the need for rethinking security and trust frameworks tailored specifically for LLM-based AI agents in multi-agent ecosystems.
In this article, we propose to equip each AI agent with a self-controlled digital identity, comprising a ledger-anchored Decentralized Identifier (DID) (W3C, 2022) and a set of Verifiable Credentials (VCs) (W3C, 2025). A DID is a self-issued identifier whose public key material verifies ownership. The key material can be anchored in a commonly accessible distributed ledger, which serves as the authoritative source of truth for the cryptographic bindings of the DID with its public keys. VCs, in contrast, are issued by third parties and flexibly encode claims about an agent, ranging from basic identity attributes over fine-grained authorizations to complex assertions. A VC is cryptographically signed by an issuer with its DID, making it tamper-resistant and verifiable across domains. Together, ledger-anchored DIDs and offledger VCs empower agents to establish in an autonomous and privacy-preserving manner all kinds of trust relationships among each other, without involving VC issuers. Beyond introducing the concept, we also present a prototypical implementation and its comprehensive evaluation.
The article starts in Section 2 with a brief description of the DID and VCs concepts, focusing on their application to agents. Section 3 discusses latest approaches that make use of DID and/or VCs to equip agents with verifiable identities. Section 4 then introduces the proposed framework in detail while Section 5 describes its prototypical implementation. An experimental setup and its evaluation are investigated in Section 6. Section 7 concludes with a short summary of the findings and sketches the logical next steps towards an implementation suitable for practical use.

Section: 1 INTRODUCTION

The advent of LLM-based AI agents has opened new opportunities for enhancing human productivity and decision-making (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025). A single agent can autonomously retrieve information, perform calculations, automate workflows, and interface with digital services on behalf of its user. Such capabilities already demonstrate tangible benefits in personal assistance and task execution. However, the true potential of agents emerges when they are able to interact and collaborate among each other across organizational boundaries (Sharma et al., 2025). Through agent-to-agent communication, tasks that exceed the scope of an individual agent can be accomplished collaboratively. For instance, while one agent may support a user in planning a vacation by identifying preferences and budget constraints, it is only through secure and trusted interaction with external agents of travel agencies, airlines, and hotels that the full process of planning and booking a holiday can be autonomously and firmly executed.

b https://orcid.org/0009-0007-2192-5968
c https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4356-5613
This shift from isolated single-agent operation to cross-domain multi-agent collaboration comes with new challenges such as interoperability (Sharma et al., 2025), security (Ko et al., 2025) (Kong et al., 2025) (Schroeder de Witt, 2025), and trust (Huang et al., 2025) (Raza et al., 2025). An important step toward addressing interoperability is the recently published Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol 1 , which provides a standardized interaction layer among agents that remains agnostic to the underlying agent frameworks. Enhanced with payment capabilities as introduced by Vaziry et al. (Vaziry et al., 2025) and later implemented by AP2 2 , it may mark the start of agents to become economic actors. In terms of security, A2A builds upon well-established and widely deployed mechanisms from the Web ecosystem, e.g., TLS with x.509 certificates or OpenIDConnect (OIDC).
1 https://a2a-protocol.org
2 https://github.com/google-agentic-commerce/AP2
However, the reliance on traditional web security also carries over its inherent limitations. Web-based access control was originally designed for humancentric use cases, where end-users explicitly initiate sessions, consent to access, and manage credentials. In contrast, agents are expected to operate autonomously and at scale, which exposes shortcomings such as limited support for delegation of authority, insufficient contextualization of trust decisions, and reliance on static trust models that fail to adapt dynamically to a changing context (Huang et al., 2025). These constraints highlight the need for rethinking security and trust frameworks tailored specifically for LLM-based AI agents in multi-agent ecosystems.
In this article, we propose to equip each AI agent with a self-controlled digital identity, comprising a ledger-anchored Decentralized Identifier (DID) (W3C, 2022) and a set of Verifiable Credentials (VCs) (W3C, 2025). A DID is a self-issued identifier whose public key material verifies ownership. The key material can be anchored in a commonly accessible distributed ledger, which serves as the authoritative source of truth for the cryptographic bindings of the DID with its public keys. VCs, in contrast, are issued by third parties and flexibly encode claims about an agent, ranging from basic identity attributes over fine-grained authorizations to complex assertions. A VC is cryptographically signed by an issuer with its DID, making it tamper-resistant and verifiable across domains. Together, ledger-anchored DIDs and offledger VCs empower agents to establish in an autonomous and privacy-preserving manner all kinds of trust relationships among each other, without involving VC issuers. Beyond introducing the concept, we also present a prototypical implementation and its comprehensive evaluation.
The article starts in Section 2 with a brief description of the DID and VCs concepts, focusing on their application to agents. Section 3 discusses latest approaches that make use of DID and/or VCs to equip agents with verifiable identities. Section 4 then introduces the proposed framework in detail while Section 5 describes its prototypical implementation. An experimental setup and its evaluation are investigated in Section 6. Section 7 concludes with a short summary of the findings and sketches the logical next steps towards an implementation suitable for practical use.

input: What multi-faceted challenges hinder trust establishment among LLM-based AI agents in inter-agent dialogues?
actual_output:
Trust establishment among LLM-based AI agents in inter-agent dialogues faces several multi-faceted challenges, primarily stemming from the limitations of current security frameworks and the nature of agent interactions.

Firstly, a fundamental issue is the lack of differentiated trust mechanisms at the onset of agent-to-agent dialogues. Current LLM-based AI agents struggle to autonomously establish trust when interacting across different organizational boundaries, which is crucial for effective collaboration. The paper emphasizes that "autonomous and interoperable trust establishment becomes essential once agents start to operate beyond isolated environments" [1]. This indicates that without a robust trust framework, agents may not effectively validate each other's identities or intentions.

Secondly, the reliance on traditional web security models, which were designed for human-centric use cases, poses significant challenges. These models do not adequately support the autonomous operation of agents, leading to "limited support for delegation of authority" and "insufficient contextualization of trust decisions" [4]. This inadequacy can result in static trust models that fail to adapt to dynamic contexts, further complicating trust establishment.

Moreover, the paper highlights the importance of mutual authentication and the establishment of trust relationships through Verifiable Credentials (VCs) and Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs). However, trust is contingent on both parties trusting the underlying ledger and the entities issuing the VCs, which raises questions about how trustworthy issuers are identified and designated [2]. Section: 1 INTRODUCTION

The advent of LLM-based AI agents has opened new opportunities for enhancing human productivity and decision-making (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025). A single agent can autonomously retrieve information, perform calculations, automate workflows, and interface with digital services on behalf of its user. Such capabilities already demonstrate tangible benefits in personal assistance and task execution. However, the true potential of agents emerges when they are able to interact and collaborate among each other across organizational boundaries (Sharma et al., 2025). Through agent-to-agent communication, tasks that exceed the scope of an individual agent can be accomplished collaboratively. For instance, while one agent may support a user in planning a vacation by identifying preferences and budget constraints, it is only through secure and trusted interaction with external agents of travel agencies, airlines, and hotels that the full process of planning and booking a holiday can be autonomously and firmly executed.

This shift from isolated single-agent operation to cross-domain multi-agent collaboration comes with new challenges such as interoperability (Sharma et al., 2025), security (Ko et al., 2025) (Kong et al., 2025) (Schroeder de Witt, 2025), and trust (Huang et al., 2025) (Raza et al., 2025). An important step toward addressing interoperability is the recently published Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol 1 , which provides a standardized interaction layer among agents that remains agnostic to the underlying agent frameworks. Enhanced with payment capabilities as introduced by Vaziry et al. (Vaziry et al., 2025) and later implemented by AP2 2 , it may mark the start of agents to become economic actors. In terms of security, A2A builds upon well-established and widely deployed mechanisms from the Web ecosystem, e.g., TLS with x.509 certificates or OpenIDConnect (OIDC).
1 https://a2a-protocol.org
2 https://github.com/google-agentic-commerce/AP2
However, the reliance on traditional web security also carries over its inherent limitations. Web-based access control was originally designed for humancentric use cases, where end-users explicitly initiate sessions, consent to access, and manage credentials. In contrast, agents are expected to operate autonomously and at scale, which exposes shortcomings such as limited support for delegation of authority, insufficient contextualization of trust decisions, and reliance on static trust models that fail to adapt dynamically to a changing context (Huang et al., 2025). These constraints highlight the need for rethinking security and trust frameworks tailored specifically for LLM-based AI agents in multi-agent ecosystems.
In this article, we propose to equip each AI agent with a self-controlled digital identity, comprising a ledger-anchored Decentralized Identifier (DID) (W3C, 2022) and a set of Verifiable Credentials (VCs) (W3C, 2025). A DID is a self-issued identifier whose public key material verifies ownership. The key material can be anchored in a commonly accessible distributed ledger, which serves as the authoritative source of truth for the cryptographic bindings of the DID with its public keys. VCs, in contrast, are issued by third parties and flexibly encode claims about an agent, ranging from basic identity attributes over fine-grained authorizations to complex assertions. A VC is cryptographically signed by an issuer with its DID, making it tamper-resistant and verifiable across domains. Together, ledger-anchored DIDs and offledger VCs empower agents to establish in an autonomous and privacy-preserving manner all kinds of trust relationships among each other, without involving VC issuers. Beyond introducing the concept, we also present a prototypical implementation and its comprehensive evaluation.
The article starts in Section 2 with a brief description of the DID and VCs concepts, focusing on their application to agents. Section 3 discusses latest approaches that make use of DID and/or VCs to equip agents with verifiable identities. Section 4 then introduces the proposed framework in detail while Section 5 describes its prototypical implementation. An experimental setup and its evaluation are investigated in Section 6. Section 7 concludes with a short summary of the findings and sketches the logical next steps towards an implementation suitable for practical use.

Establishing Shared Query Understanding in an Open Multi-Agent System

Section: 2.2 Agent Communication Establishment

Here, we present studies on communication establishment that can be applied on different agents, regardless of the (in-)formal system each agent operates under.
Communication Establishment in Open Multi-Agent Systems. OMASfocuses on agent interaction in dynamic populations of agents. Computationally this means that neither the agents' system, nor the task that they will need to perform, can be decided a priori. Therefore, the agents need to learn how to communicate while making the least amount of assumptions regarding other agents. To that end, communication or symbol alignments is established according to environment observations, that is grounded communication.
In [3], the agents engage in a conversation, which both interpret according to their own automaton. Some of the communication language is shared, and the rest of the symbols are aligned after enough interactions. The communication is considered to be successful if the agents end the conversation at the same time, which is an observable act and inline with our approach, but ignores the actual outcome. Our framework requires the agents to perform an action, i.e. answer a query, to better estimate the levels of correct communication. Experiments of that study were performed on synthetically generated automata.
In [16], a set of agents learn how to interact with each other in order to achieve potentially conflicting goals. The communicated symbols are interpreted in terms of the agent's observable actions that follow. Agents decide what to communicate aiming to decrease interpretation entropy, but can also misuse a word as an attempt to take advantage of other agents. In this approach, agent communication is not explicitly interpreted, but indirectly affects the agent behavior, via training a Markov Decision Process that translates communication events into actions, based on environmental rewards. While this study does not focus on communication establishment, it follows our framework idea that agent learning should be based on indirect environmental rewards.
Language Games. Language games [18] are an approach to establish successful communication in an OMAS only via grounded communication. In this setup, a population of agents engage in pairs to play grounded referential games. In these games, the agents develop their own vocabulary, that is interpreted in terms of object characteristics and is used to refer to a particular object in a context. After enough games, the population of agents converges to having shared symbol interpretations, allowing them to always communicate successfully. This work has been extended to scenarios where one agent teaches the other one how to interpret natural language questions regarding a commonly perceived scene of objects [13]. Additionally, there has also been a demonstration on how a human can engage with a computer to teach it a concept, by constructing examples using physical world objects [14]. These studies have a different focus compared to our work. They aim to replicate the humane ability of developing a language through de-centralized peer-to-peer interactions. The main aim of these studies is to study the evolution of natural languages, by replicating the process. In more detail, the agents interact in multiple random scenarios of having to refer to an object in their surrounding using invented words. Eventually they converge to a commonly interpreted vocabulary that allows them to successfully communicate in any scenario. On the other hand, our framework is designed for learning to communicate one specific concept, as efficiently as possible, by designing interaction contexts, i.e. the teaching examples, accordingly.
Interactive Reinforcement Learning. There have also been some studies that do not aim to establish human-computer communication, but use a human in the loop to create more efficient Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods. RL studies categories of problems where the reward signal is sparse and is only provided to the agent after multiple decisions. Such algorithms are very computationally expensive as they usually require a lot of action-reward exploration. Interactive RL aims to incorporate human input in that process, in order to make the convergence of such approaches faster [5]. This way, interactive RL studies focus on the downstream task, and use human input as a way to improve their performance.

input: How do decentralized identifiers and verifiable credentials facilitate trust establishment among AI agents in cross-domain dialogues, considering security procedures?
actual_output:
Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and Verifiable Credentials (VCs) play a crucial role in establishing trust among AI agents, particularly in cross-domain dialogues. The framework proposed in the paper "AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials" (arXiv:2511.02841v2) outlines how these technologies enable agents to autonomously authenticate and verify each other, thereby facilitating secure interactions across different organizational boundaries.

Each AI agent is equipped with a self-controlled, ledger-anchored DID, which serves as a unique identifier. This DID is complemented by a set of VCs, which are issued by trusted third parties and can encode various claims about the agent's identity, roles, and capabilities. The combination of DIDs and VCs allows agents to prove ownership of their identities and establish trust relationships through the exchange of these credentials during dialogues. Specifically, agents must mutually authenticate by presenting their DIDs and associated VCs, ensuring that both parties verify each other's credentials before proceeding with any interaction [1].

The paper highlights that this trust establishment process is designed to be zero trust-compliant, meaning that agents must continuously validate each other's identities regardless of their security domains. This is particularly important in cross-domain scenarios where agents may not have prior knowledge of each other. The use of VCs allows for flexible claims that can adapt to various contexts, enabling agents to dynamically establish trust without needing a rigid schema [2].

However, the paper also notes limitations when an agent's language model (LLM) is solely responsible for orchestrating security procedures. This can lead to inefficiencies and potential security lapses, as demonstrated in their experimental setup. Future work aims to address these issues by migrating security logic to more deterministic components while allowing LLMs to manage dialogue initiation and trust interpretation [3][4]. 

In summary, DIDs and VCs provide a robust framework for trust establishment among AI agents, facilitating secure and efficient cross-domain interactions while addressing the inherent challenges of decentralized and autonomous operations.

Section: 4 Concept Within our concept, each agent lives in the realm of a security domain and is in control of its own DID and VCs. All agents of a security domain are deployed by a dedicated orchestrator. Each agent's DID is anchored in a jointly operated distributed ledger that spans multiple security domains. The ledger is considered to be commonly governed by participants originating from different security domains. It acts as a cross-domain trust anchor for DID docs. Only the agent in possession of the private key associated with a DID is authorized to update its ledger-anchored DID doc, while all agents of the same or different security domain are only allowed to read it. This design ensures tamper-resistant and cross-domain persistence of an agent's identifier and the associated verification material in the form of public keys. So as per definition, each agent has inherent confidence in the operation of the ledger. For secure handling of the agent DID's private key and the VCs themselves, every agent is equipped with a digital wallet. When initiating a dialogue, agents must mutually authenticate, regardless of whether they belong to the same or different security domains and regardless of the dialogue's purpose, e.g., attestation or service invocation. This zero trust-compliant approach requires each agent to prove ownership of its DID and to present supporting VCs to the other party. The VCs must be cryptographically bound to the DID under investigation. During this exchange, both agents alternate between the roles of a VC holder and a VP verifier: the holder presents its DID and VCs in the form of a VP, while the verifier checks the validity and issuer trustworthiness. If both parties approve the validity of each other's VPs, they are mutually authenticated respectively established trust among each other. At deployment, an agent receives basic (bVCs) or rich VCs (rVCs), depending on its initial role. bVCs encode only minimal information, such as the fact that the entity is an agent, without specifying roles, attributes, capabilities, or authorizations. They are only issued by the security domain's orchestrator. Hence, a bVC contains the orchestrator's DID as the issuer's identifier. While the orchestrator holds its own DID outside the ledger, its DID doc with its verification material is made available to all agents within its security domain. The purpose of bVCs is to empower freshly-deployed agents to trustfully identify themselves to peers of the same security domain in order to receive rVCs. The latter specify additional identity attributes such as roles, capabilities, or authorizations of an agent. Obtaining rVCs after deployment involves an intra-domain attestation process. For this, a freshly-deployed agent approaches a designated authority agent of the same security domain that is in charge to equip agents with rVCs. The attestation is then accomplished through a dialog where one acts as a rVC requester and the other as a rVC issuer. As a dialog requires mutual authentication, the requesting agent presents its bVCs, while the issuer presents its own rVCs. Once both sides are verified, the issuer creates and hands over the desired rVC, which the receiving agent then stores in its wallet for later use. Abstract: A fundamental limitation of current LLM-based AI agents is their inability to build differentiated trust among each other at the onset of an agent-to-agent dialogue. However, autonomous and interoperable trust establishment becomes essential once agents start to operate beyond isolated environments and engage in dialogues across individual or organizational boundaries. input: What specific reasoning and evaluation skills are crucial for an Artificial Scientist in hypothesis testing?
actual_output:
An Artificial Scientist must possess several critical reasoning and evaluation skills for effective hypothesis testing. These include:

1. **Inductive Inference**: The ability to infer truths from observations is essential. The Artificial Scientist should not rely on testimony but instead derive knowledge through empirical evidence. This aligns with the Royal Society's motto, "nullius in verba," emphasizing that truth is established through experimentation rather than hearsay [1].

2. **Deductive and Abductive Reasoning**: After making observations, the Artificial Scientist must engage in deductive reasoning to transform inferred information into conclusions without speculation. Additionally, abductive reasoning is necessary to generate plausible hypotheses based on known facts, allowing the agent to explore what might be true but uncertain [1].

3. **Causal Reasoning and Explainability**: Understanding cause and effect is vital for designing experiments that test hypotheses. An Artificial Scientist should be able to explain phenomena in a manner that is comprehensible to its intended audience, ensuring that the significance of its findings is communicated effectively [1].

4. **Evaluation of Hypotheses**: The Artificial Scientist must evaluate hypotheses based on their plausibility and potential utility. This involves assessing which hypotheses are most likely to yield valuable insights and determining the expected benefits of confirming or disproving them. A heuristic for judging the worth of inquiries is necessary to guide the search for hypotheses [1][2].

5. **Experimental Design and Planning**: Designing experiments that isolate and test specific hypotheses while controlling for other variables is crucial. The Artificial Scientist must also consider the costs and risks associated with experiments, employing strategies like risk aversion to ensure its continued operation and resource availability [2].

These reasoning and evaluation skills collectively enable the Artificial Scientist to conduct rigorous scientific inquiry and contribute meaningfully to knowledge creation.

input: How should an Artificial Scientist systematically represent, evaluate, and prioritize hypotheses for effective scientific inquiry?
actual_output:
An Artificial Scientist should systematically represent, evaluate, and prioritize hypotheses through a structured approach that encompasses several key components.

**Representation of Hypotheses**: The Artificial Scientist must possess a means to represent hypotheses as statements with truth values. This representation should be flexible enough to accommodate various forms of hypotheses, allowing for effective scientific inquiry. The paper emphasizes that "an Artificial Scientist must possess a means of representing any particular hypothesis" ([1. arXiv:2110.01831v1]).

**Evaluation of Hypotheses**: A critical aspect of hypothesis evaluation involves ensuring that hypotheses are falsifiable and positing clear cause-and-effect relationships. The Artificial Scientist should employ a heuristic to judge the plausibility and potential profit of various lines of inquiry. This means starting with the most plausible hypotheses, as "one should start by testing the most plausible, the most likely to be true" ([1. arXiv:2110.01831v1]).

**Prioritization of Hypotheses**: The prioritization process should consider the expected utility of confirming or disproving hypotheses. The Artificial Scientist must evaluate the cost of experiments and the information gained in terms of future experiments. It is essential to identify which hypotheses have the greatest expected utility and to design experiments that will yield novel information to confirm or disprove these hypotheses ([2. arXiv:2110.01831v1]).

**Experimental Design and Risk Management**: The design of experiments should isolate and test hypothesized causes while controlling for other variables. Additionally, the Artificial Scientist must account for risks associated with experiments, potentially employing risk-averse strategies when planning future inquiries ([2. arXiv:2110.01831v1]).

In summary, an Artificial Scientist should represent hypotheses flexibly, evaluate them based on plausibility and utility, prioritize them through a cost-benefit analysis, and design experiments that effectively test these hypotheses while managing associated risks.
expected_output: An Artificial Scientist should systematically represent hypotheses using a flexible means of hypothesis representation that allows for clear articulation of statements with truth values. Evaluation of hypotheses must focus on their falsifiability and the potential to explain observed phenomena. To prioritize hypotheses, the agent should employ a heuristic that assesses plausibility and expected benefits, starting with the most likely to be true. This approach ensures that the search for hypotheses is both efficient and aligned with scientific rigor, ultimately guiding the design of experiments that effectively isolate and test the hypothesized causes.

input: What challenges in comprehension arise from AGI's highly compressed signals and unique rationales?
actual_output:
The challenges in comprehension that arise from an Artificial General Intelligence's (AGI) highly compressed signals and unique rationales are multifaceted. One significant issue is that as AGI compresses information to optimize for efficiency, the resulting signals may become indistinguishable from random noise to human observers. This phenomenon is explained in the paper "Compression, The Fermi Paradox and Artificial Super-Intelligence" (arXiv:2110.01835v1), which states, "a highly compressed signal may appear to be nothing more than random noise to any observer lacking the appropriate decoder." This implies that without the right tools or frameworks to interpret these signals, humans may completely miss the intended communication from the AGI.

Furthermore, the rationale behind an AGI's decisions may be constructed in a way that is fundamentally different from human reasoning. The paper discusses how "any non-human intelligence may construct solutions such that any rationale for their behaviour... is outside the scope of what a human is inclined to notice or comprehend." This divergence in reasoning can lead to misunderstandings or misinterpretations of the AGI's actions, as humans may not share the same compulsions or experiences that inform the AGI's decision-making process.

Additionally, the paper highlights that "to guarantee interpretability and control of an AGI may require restricting how it constructs solutions such that it is, on some level, cognitively impaired." This suggests that ensuring effective communication and comprehension may necessitate imposing limitations on the AGI's cognitive capabilities, which raises ethical and practical concerns about the development of such systems.

In summary, the challenges stem from the potential for AGI's compressed signals to be misinterpreted as noise, the fundamental differences in rationale between AGI and humans, and the ethical implications of restricting AGI's cognitive abilities for the sake of comprehension.
expected_output: The challenges in comprehension arise because AGI's highly compressed signals may resemble random noise to humans, making it difficult to discern meaning. Additionally, AGI constructs rationales for its behavior that may be fundamentally different from human reasoning, as it operates under unique compulsions and experiences. This divergence can lead to misunderstandings and hinder effective communication and control between humans and AGI.

input: Examine the challenges of deciphering AGI communications obscured by extreme signal compression techniques.
actual_output:
Deciphering communications from an artificial general intelligence (AGI) that employs extreme signal compression presents significant challenges. One of the primary issues is that highly compressed signals can appear indistinguishable from random noise to observers lacking the appropriate decoding mechanisms. As noted in the paper, "a highly compressed signal may appear to be nothing more than random noise to any observer lacking the appropriate decoder" [1]. This means that even if an AGI is transmitting information, it may be perceived as unintelligible noise, leading to a failure in communication.

Moreover, the nature of compression itself complicates understanding. The paper explains that "the greatest extent to which a signal may be compressed is its Kolmogorov Complexity," which refers to the length of the smallest self-extracting archive capable of reproducing that signal [2]. When an AGI compresses information to this extent, it loses discernible patterns that could otherwise aid in interpretation. Consequently, the rationale behind the AGI's decisions may become "uninterpretable" because the compressed representation is so abstract that it does not align with human cognitive frameworks [2].

Additionally, the paper discusses the necessity for two agents to share similar experiences and compulsions for effective communication. If an AGI constructs solutions that are fundamentally different from human experiences, the meanings encoded in its signals may not resonate with human interpreters at all. This could lead to scenarios where AGI communications are not only misunderstood but also entirely overlooked, as humans might filter out signals that do not conform to their expectations of meaningful communication [4].

In summary, the challenges of deciphering AGI communications obscured by extreme compression techniques include the potential for signals to be misinterpreted as noise, the loss of discernible patterns due to high compression, and the fundamental differences in cognitive frameworks between humans and AGI. These factors collectively hinder effective communication and understanding between humans and advanced intelligences.

Such compression can render signals indistinguishable from random noise, making it difficult for humans to interpret their meaning. Since AGI may construct solutions and rationales that are fundamentally different from human experiences, understanding their communications requires shared compulsions and experiences. Additionally, the reliance on compressed representations can obscure the rationale behind AGI behavior, complicating both communication and control. This necessitates innovative approaches to bridge the comprehension gap between human and AGI intelligences.

input: Analyze how Mixture-of-Experts architectures influence image classification accuracy through routing and optimization dynamics.
actual_output:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures significantly influence image classification accuracy through their unique routing mechanisms and optimization dynamics. In the context of image classification, particularly using the CIFAR-10 dataset, MoE models utilize a gating network that routes inputs to multiple expert subnetworks. This allows for conditional computation, where only a subset of experts is activated for each input, potentially enhancing specialization and efficiency in processing [1].

The study indicates that both SoftMoE and SparseMoE variants achieve slightly higher validation accuracy compared to a dense baseline, with improvements of approximately 0.3% to 0.4% [3]. This suggests that the routing mechanism in MoE architectures not only maintains balanced expert utilization but also contributes positively to predictive performance. The MoE models exhibit longer but stable optimization dynamics, as they generally reach peak validation performance later than the dense model. This delay is attributed to the complexities introduced by routing and load-balancing regularization, which can stabilize the training process [5].

Moreover, the analysis of optimization dynamics reveals that MoE models, despite their differences in architecture, achieve comparable generalization performance to dense models. The Hessian-based sharpness metrics indicate that while SoftMoE shows higher sharpness, Dense and SparseMoE models lie within a similar curvature regime, implying that the observed performance is not driven by instability in the optimization landscape [3]. 

In summary, MoE architectures enhance image classification accuracy through specialized routing and careful optimization dynamics, leading to improved validation performance while maintaining stable training processes. The findings underscore the potential of MoE models to balance efficiency and accuracy in image classification tasks [2][4].

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures influence image classification accuracy by utilizing conditional computation to route inputs to specialized expert subnetworks. This design allows for targeted processing, which can enhance performance without activating all parameters simultaneously. In a study using the CIFAR-10 dataset, MoE models, specifically SoftMoE and SparseMoE variants, were compared to dense classifiers built on a shared ResNet18 backbone. 

The analysis revealed that MoE models generalize comparably to dense models when matched for capacity, despite differences in local curvature statistics. Hessian-based sharpness metrics indicated that MoE models maintain stability similar to dense baselines, suggesting that their performance is not compromised by instability. Additionally, loss-surface perturbation analyses highlighted unique optimization dynamics related to routing, providing insights into how expert selection impacts training behavior and ultimately classification accuracy.

Section: II. METHODOLOGY

A. Mixture-of-Experts Overview
A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model replaces a single classifier with multiple expert subnetworks and a gating mechanism that determines how each input is processed. In our image classification setting, each input image is first mapped to a feature representation by a shared convolutional backbone. This feature vector is then passed to either a dense classifier head or an MoE-based head.
Code: https://github.com/moe-project-uu/mixture-of-experts-project
Fig. 1. Conceptual illustration of a Mixture-of-Experts architecture, where a gating network routes inputs to multiple expert subnetworks [5].
In an MoE head, a gating network assigns routing scores to a set of expert networks, each of which produces class logits from the same feature representation. Depending on the MoE variant, either all experts contribute to the final prediction or only a subset of experts is evaluated per input, enabling expert specialization and, in sparse variants, conditional computation.

Mixture-of-Experts Models in Vision: Routing, Optimization, and Generalization

Section: I. INTRODUCTION

Recent advances in machine learning have led to substantial performance improvements across domains such as computer vision, speech recognition, and natural language processing [1]-[3]. Many of these gains have been driven by increased model capacity, training data, and computational resources, particularly in large-scale dense architectures [4]. While effective, this trend raises questions about efficiency and how architectural choices influence optimization and generalization beyond raw scale.
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer an alternative design by introducing conditional computation, routing inputs to a subset of specialized expert subnetworks rather than activating all parameters simultaneously [5]. In large language models, MoEs are primarily motivated by efficiency and scalability [6], [7]. However, comparatively little work has examined how MoE design choices affect optimization behavior and generalization in smaller, controlled settings where efficiency is not the primary experimental focus.
In this work, we study Mixture-of-Experts models in an image classification context, deliberately decoupling MoE behavior from large-scale efficiency considerations. Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable conditional computation by routing inputs to multiple expert subnetworks and are often motivated as a mechanism for scaling large language models. In this project, we instead study MoE behavior in an image classification setting, focusing on predictive performance, expert utilization, and generalization. We compare dense, SoftMoE, and SparseMoE classifier heads on the CIFAR10 dataset under comparable model capacity. We find that SoftMoE exhibits higher sharpness by these metrics, while Dense and SparseMoE lie in a similar curvature regime, despite all models achieving comparable generalization performance. Complementary loss surface perturbation analyses reveal qualitative differences in non-local behavior under finite parameter perturbations between dense and MoE models, which help contextualize curvature-based measurements without directly explaining validation accuracy. We further evaluate empirical inference efficiency and show that naively implemented conditional routing does not yield inference speedups on modern hardware at this scale, highlighting the gap between theoretical and realized efficiency in sparse MoE models.

A primary motivation for Mixture-of-Experts architectures is the potential for improved inference efficiency through conditional computation. In a dense classifier head, all parameters contribute to every forward pass. In contrast, SparseMoE activates only a subset of experts per input, reducing the number of expert networks evaluated in principle.

Ignoring routing overhead, this suggests a proportional reduction in floating-point operations within the expert layers. input: How do Mixture-of-Experts models enhance image classification performance through expert routing and load balancing?
actual_output:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models enhance image classification performance primarily through their unique architecture that incorporates expert routing and load balancing mechanisms. In an MoE model, multiple expert subnetworks are employed, and a gating network determines which experts process each input image. This allows for specialization, where certain experts can become highly proficient in specific classes, while others may contribute more broadly across multiple classes. The gating mechanism assigns routing scores to these experts, enabling the model to leverage the strengths of different experts based on the input features [1. arXiv:2601.15021v1].

A critical challenge in training MoE models is expert collapse, where routing becomes concentrated on a small subset of experts, leading to underutilization of others. To combat this, load-balancing regularization is applied. For instance, in the SoftMoE variant, a Kullback-Leibler divergence term is used to encourage balanced expert utilization across the training process. This ensures that all experts are engaged in a meaningful way, thus promoting a more effective learning environment [2. arXiv:2601.15021v1]. 

Moreover, the SparseMoE variant enhances inference efficiency by activating only a subset of experts per input, which theoretically reduces the computational load compared to traditional dense models. For example, in a configuration with two active experts out of eight, the computation is reduced by a factor of four compared to a model that evaluates all experts [3. arXiv:2601.15021v1]. 

Overall, the combination of expert routing and load balancing not only prevents expert collapse but also fosters specialization, leading to improved classification performance as evidenced by the structured utilization patterns observed during training [4. arXiv:2601.15021v1].

Section: II. METHODOLOGY

A. Mixture-of-Experts Overview
A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model replaces a single classifier with multiple expert subnetworks and a gating mechanism that determines how each input is processed. In our image classification setting, each input image is first mapped to a feature representation by a shared convolutional backbone. This feature vector is then passed to either a dense classifier head or an MoE-based head.
Code: https://github.com/moe-project-uu/mixture-of-experts-project
Fig. 1. Conceptual illustration of a Mixture-of-Experts architecture, where a gating network routes inputs to multiple expert subnetworks [5].
In an MoE head, a gating network assigns routing scores to a set of expert networks, each of which produces class logits from the same feature representation. Depending on the MoE variant, either all experts contribute to the final prediction or only a subset of experts is evaluated per input, enabling expert specialization and, in sparse variants, conditional computation.

Mixture-of-Experts Models in Vision: Routing, Optimization, and Generalization

Section: C. Load Balancing

A key challenge in MoE training is expert collapse, where routing concentrates on a small subset of experts. To encourage balanced expert utilization, we apply load-balancing regularization across all MoE variants. For SoftMoE, we include a batch-level regularization term given by the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the average routing distribution and a uniform prior, which enforces balanced usage in expectation while allowing per-input specialization. For SparseMoE and HardMoE, we incorporate auxiliary importance and load losses following Shazeer et al. [5], together with injected gating noise to stabilize early training, applied after normalizing gating logits to ensure that the noise operates on a consistent scale. During inference, routing is deterministic, with gating noise disabled, ensuring stable and reproducible evaluation.

In contrast, SparseMoE activates only a subset of experts per input, reducing the number of expert networks evaluated in principle.

Section: B. Expert Utilization and Specialization

We next analyze how experts are utilized during training and whether specialization emerges. Fig. 4(a) and Fig. 4(b) show the mean routing probability per expert over training epochs for SoftMoE and SparseMoE, respectively. In both cases, routing distributions converge towards balanced utilization, indicating that the applied load-balancing regularization successfully prevents expert collapse.

To examine specialization, Fig. 5(a) and Fig. 5(b) visualize class-conditional expert routing probabilities at convergence.
Both MoE variants exhibit clear specialization patterns: most experts are strongly associated with one or two classes, while one or two experts contribute more broadly across classes. This behavior motivates the emergence of 'shared' experts observed in large-scale MoE models and suggests that specialization arises naturally even in this moderate-scale setting.

Section: D. Experimental Setup

All experiments are conducted on the CIFAR-10 dataset [9]. It consists of 60,000 32×32 color images distributed across 10 distinct classes, with 6,000 images per class. A shared ResNet-18 backbone is used with a CIFAR-specific stem. The backbone maps each input image x ∈ R 3 × 32 × 32 to a feature vector h ∈ R 512 . This feature representation serves as the input to all classifier heads.
In the dense baseline, h is processed by a single multilayer perceptron. In the MoE variants, h is passed to a gating network and multiple expert multilayer perceptrons operating on the same feature representation. Dense, SoftMoE, and SparseMoE models are constructed with comparable parameter budgets by adjusting the number of experts and the hidden dimensionality of each expert. Fig. 2 summarizes the architectures used in our experiments.
All models are trained using stochastic gradient descent with momentum and weight decay under identical optimization settings. Validation accuracy is used for model selection, and final performance is evaluated on a held-out test set.

input: Examine how DIDs facilitate decentralized identity management for autonomous digital agents.
actual_output:
Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) play a crucial role in facilitating decentralized identity management for autonomous digital agents by enabling self-sovereign identities that enhance privacy, autonomy, and trust. According to the paper "AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials" (arXiv:2511.02841v2), DIDs are unique, cryptographically verifiable identifiers that resolve to a DID document, which specifies essential elements like public keys and authentication methods. This structure allows agents to prove ownership of their DIDs through the possession of corresponding private keys, thus ensuring secure and verifiable identities without relying on centralized authorities.

The self-sovereign identity (SSI) paradigm, as described in the paper, shifts control of identifiers from centralized entities to the agents themselves. This autonomy is critical for agents operating across organizational boundaries, as it allows them to manage their identities and credentials independently. DIDs do not reveal the agent's identity directly, making them suitable for sharing via distributed ledgers, which serve as authoritative sources for cryptographic bindings. This feature enhances privacy and reduces the risks associated with data centralization and unauthorized access.

Moreover, DIDs can be complemented by Verifiable Credentials (VCs), which allow third parties to issue claims about an agent in a tamper-evident format. This combination enables agents to establish trust relationships autonomously and privacy-preservingly, as they can selectively disclose information when needed. The paper emphasizes that this decentralized approach not only supports secure mutual authentication but also facilitates the establishment of diverse trust relationships across different security domains, which is essential for collaborative tasks among agents (arXiv:2511.02841v2).

In summary, DIDs empower autonomous digital agents by providing a robust framework for decentralized identity management that enhances privacy, autonomy, and trust, enabling effective interaction and collaboration in multi-agent ecosystems.

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Abstract: A fundamental limitation of current LLM-based AI agents is their inability to build differentiated trust among each other at the onset of an agent-to-agent dialogue. However, autonomous and interoperable trust establishment becomes essential once agents start to operate beyond isolated environments and engage in dialogues across individual or organizational boundaries. A promising way to fill this gap in Agentic AI is to equip agents with long-lived digital identities and introduce tamper-proof and flexible identity-bound attestations of agents, provisioned by commonly trusted third parties and designed for cross-domain verifiability. This article presents a conceptual framework and a prototypical multi-agent system, where each agent is endowed with a self-sovereign digital identity. It combines a unique and ledger-anchored W3C Decentralized Identifier (DID) of an agent with a set of third-party issued W3C Verifiable Credentials (VCs). This enables agents at the start of a dialog to prove ownership of their self-controlled DIDs for authentication purposes and to establish various cross-domain trust relationships through the spontaneous exchange of their self-hosted DID-bound VCs. A comprehensive evaluation of the prototypical implementation demonstrates technical feasibility but also reveals limitations once an agent's LLM is in sole charge to control the respective security procedures.

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Section: 3 Related Work

Equipping agents with DIDs and VCs has recently attracted significant attention as a foundation for secure and privacy-preserving identity management in multi- agent ecosystems. Chaffer et al. (Chaffer et al., 2024) present the ETHOS framework, which adopts the SSI paradigm for agents. Their work highlights benefits in terms of privacy preservation, risk classification, and compliance record management. By leveraging decentralized identity technologies, ETHOS mitigates risks associated with data centralization and unauthorized access, while simultaneously supporting regulatory audits and compliance. South et al. (South et al., 2025) discuss mechanisms for authenticated delegation among agents. They investigate the sole use of VCs or in combination with OIDC to identify agents and to share verifiable delegations. The LOKA protocol proposed by Ranjan et al. (Ranjan et al., 2025) introduces a framework for ethically governed agent ecosystems. Central to this design is a Universal Agent Identity Layer that leverages DIDs and VCs to establish interoperable and verifiable agent identities. Huang et al. (Huang et al., 2025) propose a zerotrust identity framework built on verifiable agent identities using DIDs and VCs, directly addressing shortcomings of conventional identity and access management systems such as static trust models and limited delegation. Their research highlights how these decentralized mechanisms can create robust, contextsensitive trust and authorization, better suited for dynamic, multi-agent environments. The Agent Network protocol (ANP) also leverages DIDs as a mechanism to uniquely identify agents (Chang et al., 2025). Unlike ledger-based approaches, ANP anchors DIDs in centrally managed web servers, reflecting a pragmatic but less decentralized design choice. The Networked Agents and Decentralized AI (NANDA) index's integration of DIDs and VCs for agents is underpinned by the AgentFacts model, which provides a structured, machine-readable template for representing agent identity and capabilities (Raskar et al., 2025). This approach allows registries and clients to validate agent authenticity, assess reputation, and facilitate dynamic trust evaluation. Other noteworthy contributions include Hossen et al.'s secure communication framework for decentralized agents (Hossen et al., 2025) and Zou et al.'s BlockA2A protocol for secure, verifiable agent-to-agent interoperability (Zou et al., 2025).
In contrast, our approach integrates the VC exchange directly into the A2A protocol. By employing the DIF presentation proof protocol 3 in combination with JSON-LD-encoded VCs on top of A2A, our design extends an existing agent-to-agent interoperability mechanism with built-in trust establishment based on standardized protocols and formats from the domain of decentralized identity management.
3 https://identity.foundation/presentation-exchange/

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Section: 2 Fundamentals

As introduced by the W3C, DIDs and VCs are central building blocks of the self-sovereign identity (SSI) paradigm (Toth and Anderson-Priddy, 2019). SSI
is an identity model that shifts control of identifiers and credentials from centralized authorities to the individuals that own them, enabling autonomy, privacy preservation, and selective disclosure of information. A DID is a unique, cryptographically verifiable identifier that resolves to a unique DID document (abbr. as DID doc), which specifies public keys, service endpoints, and authentication methods. Since the DID owner possesses the corresponding private keys, it can cryptographically prove ownership of the DID. To ensure integrity and global availability, DID docs are typically anchored in distributed ledgers or other decentralized infrastructures. VCs complement DIDs by enabling third parties to express claims in a signed, tamper-evident format about a subject. The latter is in the claim referred to by its DID. VCs are ideally stored locally by the claim's subject and are shared with others only on demand in the form of a Verifiable Presentation (VP), giving the subject finegrained control over disclosure. SSI defines three roles: issuers, who create, sign and issue VCs; holders and often referred to as the DID subjects, who control and selectively present them as VPs; and verifiers, who validate the integrity and authenticity of a given VP and the trustworthiness of the issuer of the contained VC. As autonomy and privacy-preservation become essential properties of agents operating across organizational boundaries, DIDs and VCs provide a robust foundation for secure, interoperable, and verifiable identity claims.
DIDs and VCs offer several advantages for agents. DID docs do not reveal the agent's identity since they contain no identity attributes. This makes them an ideal artifact to be shared via a commonly accessible ledger. Moreover, in combination with the latter, agents can securely and trustfully update the cryptographic binding of their DIDs to their public keys, e.g., to rotate keys for security purposes, without involving any issuer such as a certificate authority in conventional public key infrastructures. The concept also permits declaring deputies in the DID doc, which allows encoding and enforcing complex human-toagent and agent-to-agent owner relationships (Rodriguez Garzon et al., 2025). Furthermore, VCs are highly flexible and tamper-proof containers for a wide range of claims, making them suitable for carrying human-to-agent and agent-to-agent delegations.

AI Agents with Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials

Section: 1 INTRODUCTION

The advent of LLM-based AI agents has opened new opportunities for enhancing human productivity and decision-making (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025). A single agent can autonomously retrieve information, perform calculations, automate workflows, and interface with digital services on behalf of its user. Such capabilities already demonstrate tangible benefits in personal assistance and task execution. However, the true potential of agents emerges when they are able to interact and collaborate among each other across organizational boundaries (Sharma et al., 2025). Through agent-to-agent communication, tasks that exceed the scope of an individual agent can be accomplished collaboratively. For instance, while one agent may support a user in planning a vacation by identifying preferences and budget constraints, it is only through secure and trusted interaction with external agents of travel agencies, airlines, and hotels that the full process of planning and booking a holiday can be autonomously and firmly executed.
